title: The Philippine immigration detention center: don't pay, and your deportation never moves
dek: A Chinese surfer held for 41 days in the Philippines saw not a prison but a business with prices on everything: a bed, a boxed meal, a phone, a lawyer's fee. Those who don't pay stay for years, sometimes more than a decade.
why: StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is one man's ordeal; the real value is in the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, and lawyers raising their prices on the spot.
who: Founders and overseas-expansion operators interested in the situation of Chinese abroad, the Philippine business environment, and the machinery of gray industry and immigration corruption.
skip: 6:29-9:14 — the surfing career and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: The immigration bureau quoted 1.5 million pesos to walk free on the spot
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, immigration officials pulled him aside and said quietly, "I can help you." After talking to a lawyer, the word came back: give 1.5 million pesos, about 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can be released immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 or 13 people picked up in the same sweep, nobody agreed to pay. Everyone thought something like this couldn't possibly still exist in 2026 and wanted to resolve it through normal legal procedure. But the price of refusing was this: they were moved from the holding cells of the General City police station to the immigration bureau's main detention center in Manila, where Feili ended up staying 41 days.

points.h: When his phone was confiscated, the money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained his phone was taken, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was normal procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days he applied repeatedly and couldn't get the phone back; only after he kept pressuring the Chinese consulate and a lawyer was it returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer history showed money had been sent out — then sent back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in it. Feili says it wasn't about the amount; it was that the phone had been handled by someone while it wasn't in his hands. His read: many Chinese doing gray-industry scams in Manila go through this same shakedown after arrest, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate, because their phones hold a mass of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout the immigration bureau promised exist — in another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own tickets to transfer, the immigration bureau works on them in shifts, saying conditions at the Manila bureau are excellent: air conditioning, plenty of freedom, a gym, basketball, takeout delivery, phones. Feili says they weren't lying — there really is air conditioning, you really can order takeout, it's just another form, a completely different form. They arrived at the main detention center past three in the morning. What he saw after getting out of the vehicle was a square area wrapped in a layer of iron grating under a sheet-metal roof, ringed by dog-cage-like iron cages, and inside them long communal platforms holding several hundred people. Past three in the morning, many weren't sleeping — bare-chested, in nothing but underwear, they clung to the cage bars to stare at the newcomers. Feili says he and the other foreigners said nothing for several minutes, then it hit them: the immigration bureau had lied to them.

points.h: The detention center is a business funded by a Chinese boss
points.body: The story Feili heard inside was that this immigration detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss in cooperation with the immigration bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were all newly built by that Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese who came in had to pay. The cheapest communal-platform bed was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy pan bosses and gambling kingpins could pay 50,000 pesos a month, over 6,000 RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — actually the same bed, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a styrofoam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan pulling the cold air into the bed. That is where the immigration bureau's promise of "air conditioning inside" came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were their investment and there was no way to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, he'd come here to serve time, how could he be expected to pay on top of that. The gang boss said with a threatening tone: you're already in here and you don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run by gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes everything Chinese inmates eat, wear and use, running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center holds about 200 people; when Feili arrived it was the low season, and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's staff draw wages — the head cook 10,000 pesos a month, the kitchen helper 5,000 — very low wages, but many people can't get out precisely because they have no money for a lawyer and can only work to earn some.

points.h: A man from Yunnan held over a year; his family thought he died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken and he was dragged into a compound to run telecom scams, and when his numbers were bad his supervisor shocked him with a stun baton every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the immigration detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own ticket, and you're gone — but the immigration bureau, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up a long time, and without paying the procedure doesn't move. He'd already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he had died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese and translated it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese man got to see the warden, who had a guard bring Feili's phone so the young man could add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. After that the immigration bureau bought a basic phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The only Chinese Feili talked with much came from a scam company whose 70 or 80 people were surrounded by the immigration bureau together with the police and the NBI, three agencies at once. The first shakedown was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet — no cameras in there — and stripping them of everything valuable. The second was the immigration bureau negotiating with the company boss over ransoms, with different quotes per person: 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos, depending on the mood of whoever was in charge. That company's deal was 3 million pesos a head, over 300,000 RMB. The boss ended up ransoming 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; his best month brought in 2 million RMB, and he'd bought a house and a car in his small home county. Later a friend kidnapped him, tens of thousands in cash was transferred away, and a crooked cop pinned an illegal gun-possession charge on him, so he couldn't leave.

points.h: A Philippine lawyer raises his price the moment he sees a Chinese client
points.body: In Cebu, through an introduction from a Lithuanian, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, over 20,000 RMB, to settle it in four weeks. After Feili reached Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and raised the price on the spot, saying that was the old price and the new price required another 120,000 pesos, over 10,000 RMB. Feili decided not to use him and wrote off the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted over 30,000 RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili says the genuinely reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedure inside out, because everyone locked up in there is Chinese. In the end he was held a bit over 30 days, 41 days counting Cebu. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili messaged him.

quotes.text: Give him 1.5 million pesos now and he can release you immediately, and you'll have no problem at all.
But it's not about how much money it was — while the phone wasn't in my hands, someone transferred money out.

Look at his corrupt bureaucratic system and its people as separate things. I still believe Filipinos are by nature very good people. But the bureaucratic system is truly too corrupt — the kind of bureaucratic system that drinks blood, human blood.
